reference.source: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
clinicalPearls: Benign Schwann-cell tumour arising most often from the vestibular division of the eighth cranial nerve within the internal auditory meatus
Classically presents with unilateral or asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, sometimes with imbalance rather than true rotatory vertigo
Any unexplained asymmetric sensorineural loss or unilateral tinnitus warrants imaging to exclude a retrocochlear lesion
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are pathognomonic of neurofibromatosis type 2 and prompt genetic evaluation, especially in younger patients
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory meatus is the gold-standard diagnostic test; enhancing tumour may expand into the cerebellopontine angle
Facial nerve function is typically preserved until tumours are large, whereas early facial weakness should raise suspicion of an alternative pathology such as a facial nerve schwannoma
Large tumours can cause trigeminal sensory loss, cerebellar signs, brainstem compression and hydrocephalus
Management options include surveillance imaging, microsurgical resection, or stereotactic radiosurgery, chosen by tumour size, growth, hearing and patient factors
reference.pathophysiology: Vestibular schwannomas are slow-growing benign neoplasms of Schwann cells, usually originating at the transition zone of the vestibular nerve near the internal auditory meatus. Growth within the confined meatus compresses adjacent auditory and vestibular fibres and their blood supply, producing progressive sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular symptoms. As the tumour enlarges it extends medially into the cerebellopontine angle, where it may compress the trigeminal and facial nerves, the cerebellum and eventually the brainstem, and obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow. Most are sporadic and unilateral; biallelic inactivation of the NF2 tumour-suppressor gene underlies both sporadic tumours and the bilateral tumours of neurofibromatosis type 2.
additionalDifferentials: Epidermoid or arachnoid cyst of the cerebellopontine angle
Sudden or idiopathic asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss
additionalInvestigations: Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory meatus and cerebellopontine angle
Pure-tone and speech audiometry documenting asymmetric sensorineural loss and speech discrimination
Auditory brainstem response testing where MRI is contraindicated
Vestibular function testing (caloric or video head impulse) to assess the affected nerve
Genetic assessment for NF2 when tumours are bilateral or the patient is young
redFlags: Rapidly progressive symptoms, severe headache or reduced consciousness suggesting brainstem compression or hydrocephalus
Cerebellar signs such as ataxia, dysmetria or nystagmus indicating a large cerebellopontine angle mass
Trigeminal sensory loss or facial weakness signalling significant tumour extension
Bilateral tumours or a family history indicating neurofibromatosis type 2
reference.prognosis: As benign tumours, vestibular schwannomas carry an excellent survival prognosis, and many small tumours remain stable under surveillance. Hearing preservation depends on tumour size and treatment, and both microsurgery and radiosurgery carry a risk to hearing and facial nerve function that rises with larger tumours; large untreated lesions can be life-threatening through brainstem compression.
pitfalls: Attributing asymmetric hearing loss or unilateral tinnitus to presbycusis or noise exposure without imaging
Assuming vertigo excludes the diagnosis, since imbalance is often subtle owing to gradual compensation
Failing to consider neurofibromatosis type 2 in young or bilateral cases
Confusing a facial nerve schwannoma with a vestibular schwannoma when facial weakness appears early
